Meriem, Janaï, Thomas : trois adolescent: Meriem, Janaï, Thomas: three teenagers from three different neighbourhoods, killed at the hands of other young people. How do we change this trajectory?
Meriem Boundaoui, Jannai Dopwell-Bailey,: Meriem Boundaoui, Jannai Dopwell-Bailey, Thomas Trudel: three teenagers killed at the hands of other young people. Illustration: Maya Sakkal
Le vendredi 19 novembre, les proches de: On Friday, Nov. 19, loved ones of Jannai Dopwell-Bailey gathered to say a final goodbye to the 16-year-old. On Oct. 18, in Côte-des-Neiges, he had been stabbed by another young person in the middle of the afternoon, after school. On Saturday, Nov. 20, the Saint-Michel neighbourhood marched in memory of Thomas Trudel, 16. The teenager was killed very close to his home in Saint-Michel, shot as he was coming back from an evening at the park with his friends. In February, Meriem Boundaoui, 15, was hit by a bullet in the head in front of a bakery in Saint-Léonard while she was with a friend. Meriem, Janaï, Thomas: three teenagers from three different neighbourhoods, killed at the hands of other young people. How do we change this trajectory?
Meriem était maghrébine, Jannai était No: Meriem was North African, Jannai was Black, Thomas was white. Although they lost their lives in similar circumstances, their tragic deaths haven’t mobilized public opinion in the same way. In the neighbourhoods, people feel that difference. Two days after Thomas’s death, Montréal’s mayor went to the site of his killing, accompanied by Montréal police chief Sylvain Caron. Ms. Plante did not go to the site where Jannai Dopwell-Bailey died. The same goes for Quebec Premier François Legault, who also laid flowers at the site of Thomas Trudel’s murder a few days after the tragedy. Neither made any statement after the death of Meriem Boundaoui or that of Jannai Dopwell-Bailey. At the funeral of the Côte-des-Neiges teenager on Nov. 20, Jannai’s loved ones denounced the unequal treatment by elected officials and institutions. Is it because these teenagers don’t look enough like their own children?
Au Forum Jeunesse de Saint-Michel, la te: At the Forum Jeunesse de Saint-Michel, tension is at its peak. Young people from the neighbourhood have gathered in the basement of the local library to make signs for a march in Thomas’s memory. They are not fooled: the group is well aware that teenagers are treated differently in the public sphere and in the media. Some wonder whether, now that the victim is white, things will change. But raising that question at the march is out of the question. “Thomas’s mother hasn’t been to the site yet; it may be the first time she’ll be at the place where her son was killed. This isn’t the time to talk about that,” says one of them. To them, Thomas was a young person like them. A young person from Saint-Michel.
<strong>Se faire justice quand on se ren: Taking justice into your own hands when everyone passes the buck
Pour préparer leurs pancartes en vue de: To prepare their signs for the march, the teenagers decide who they want to address, with the help of community workers Mohammed Mimoun and Myriam Bousksou. Some want to tell the media to stop coming to exploit their suffering and to take an interest in them only when someone dies. “You come scratch at our misery and then you leave. What do we get out of talking to you?” a young adult asks us. Others have a grudge against politicians, saying a few of them showed up at the vigil for Meriem Boundaoui, gave nice speeches and met with them, but nothing changes. “Young people are sick of repeating themselves, they’ve already talked to politicians, who just pass the buck,” they tell us. Abdellah Azzouz, 22, who used to go to the Forum Jeunesse when he was younger, is now a community worker there. “Think about what you didn’t do, or did badly, for us to end up here,” he says, looking at the federal, provincial and municipal elected officials present at the march in Thomas’s memory. In Saint-Michel, the day after Thomas died, some teenagers at the high school he attended were talking about revenge. Reda (not his real name), 16, is a student there. “These are still kids who are dying, I want all of this to stop.
Les gens étaient fâchés, je peux les com: People were angry, I can understand them. But in my opinion, that’s not the solution,” adds the student at École Joseph-François-Perreault. According to Reda, young people don’t trust the police to solve their problems. “Instead of going to the police, they prefer to keep it to themselves and go get their own justice,” he says with emotion. Reda doesn’t hide his disappointment with politicians. “I feel like they’re saying, ‘Take the money, figure it out.’ It’s as if, for them, money fixes everything. What would fix the problem is education,” he adds.
À Côte-des-Neiges, au Chalet Kent, une p: In Côte-des-Neiges, at the Chalet Kent, a photo of Jannai has been placed at the entrance of the building. This is where he recorded one of his songs. We meet teenagers who knew him, along with Karim Coppry, a youth worker and the founder of Philo-Box, an organization that offers boxing classes and discussion services to young people who frequent the chalet. The teenagers of Côte-des-Neiges say they are disappointed by the way Jannai was portrayed in some media. “People think Jannai was a bad person, but he was someone who was there for everybody. He had the same dreams as any 16-year-old. When he saw someone sad, he would cheer them up; he was a funny guy,” a 14-year-old tells us. “People see someone with dreads, they see someone with sagging pants, they think he’s a street gang member,” laments another young person, 15. The absence of the premier and the mayor at the ceremony held in memory of the Black teenager fills them with sorrow and anger. “When Jannai died, François Legault did nothing; he forgot; but when a white kid died, he went to the site. It’s like we’re worth nothing,” says one of his friends, who prefers to remain anonymous.
Comme les jeunes de Saint-Michel, ceux d: Like the young people of Saint-Michel, those of Côte-des-Neiges say they identify with their neighbourhood above all. “In Uptown, we’re a family, there’s love between us, we’re united,” they tell us. Neighbourhood culture is so present that people identify with their bus line, the 160. “When people talk about gun violence, many bring up ‘street gangs,’ but you have to understand that there’s a neighbourhood culture first and foremost,” explains Karim Coppry. The gun violence that results is rather tied to rivalries between young people from different neighbourhoods, we’re told. For the youth worker, who also grew up in the neighbourhood, the public discourse around gun violence sidesteps a central issue: poverty. The solution isn’t simple; it has to be carried out at different levels, thinks Maeli, a 13-year-old girl. “Everyone has to pitch in,” she says. Her 16-year-old friend Martin believes in a dialogue between young people from different neighbourhoods. “We’re not different, even if we come from different neighbourhoods. We’re still kids, there’s no reason to do this. We don’t want this anymore, we want more unity,” he says. Some are less optimistic. Ali, 14, doesn’t believe in change. He dreams of leaving the neighbourhood and settling in Los Angeles. “I’m going to make a lot of money and bring all my friends there,” he says when asked what he sees as a solution.
Un peu partout sur l’île, dans les quart: All over the island, in Montréal’s disadvantaged neighbourhoods, many are disillusioned. These young people no longer trust the education system or the legal system. It is hard for them to picture a future. Shana Liboul, 17, isn’t afraid of gunshots. She says she fears instead what pushes her peers to shoot at each other. “Many people struggle to understand that the young people you identify as gangsters are in fact victims. They’re in more danger than I am. Because these young people have triggers that are stronger than their thoughts. These are triggers that control them and lead them to think that what they’re doing is right,” says the teenager, who lives in Rivière-des-Prairies. Shana thinks stereotypes and discrimination push young people toward the street. “There are triggers that aren’t well understood or analyzed. It’s not the trigger under the shooter’s finger, but the hidden trigger in the back of his head that scares me. It’s what feeds his stress, his doubts, his fears, and pushes him to identify as a shooter. These triggers have no limit. They can easily hide in the back of your son’s head, my brother’s, my best friend’s, the guy at the other end of my class – it can affect anyone,” she illustrates.
« Lorsque ces jeunes vont à l’école et v: “When these young people go to school and want to become someone, but their teachers tell them they’ll never be doctors or basketball players, that’s a trigger. The scars of stereotypes hurt more than those from a bullet,” she tells us eloquently at a conference of the Coalition Pozé, a group of community workers that campaigns against violence in the neighbourhoods. “To stop these triggers from acting on many young people who live in Montréal-Nord, in Saint-Michel, in Saint-Léonard, wherever, we have to change the words, change the colour these young people see, because right now it’s just red, all they see is blood, it’s the colour of the innocent lives they take,” the teenager believes. How do we prevent that? Simply by listening, she answers. “When you take the time to listen, it can change everything,” she says.
<strong>Une radicalisation anti-système: Anti-system radicalization in the face of marginalization
Arris vit à Saint-Michel depuis deux ans: Arris has lived in Saint-Michel for two years. When Arris’s parents heard the gunshots that cost Thomas his life, they wanted to leave the neighbourhood. His father started looking, but rents in other neighbourhoods are too high. “The easiest and most radical solution is to leave the neighbourhood and leave all of this behind. But the truth is, some people can’t afford to leave. My parents can’t, and even though I don’t like the neighbourhood, and crazy stuff happens there, I just can’t afford to leave,” says the science student at Cégep de Maisonneuve. If he had the means to change things, what would he do? “If I actually had money, I’d offer it to young people first. If they fall into things like this, it’s because of boredom,” says Arris. He speaks from experience, recounting that he, too, once felt he had nothing to do to pass the time. Since then he has found things to occupy himself, between work, school and the Forum Jeunesse’s activities. “But some people didn’t get the chance to have that. They fall into illegality. Everyone who gets into illicit things, they’re all guys who are bored out of their minds,” says the young man in a shy voice.
« Il faut régaler un peu les jeunes pour: “Young people need to be treated a little so they stop being bored and getting into things like that,” adds Arris, pointing out that some don’t leave the neighbourhood, or Montréal. But beyond boredom, there is a lack of hope in the legal system. If some decide to pick up weapons and fall into illegality, it’s because they can’t see themselves in the system, the young people of the neighbourhood tell us. “We have to show young people there’s a future. We have to invest in trades, in university, in legality. And show them there’s no future in illegality. Because what do young people tell themselves? OK, they tell me I have no future, that I can’t go to that CEGEP or that university, that it’s too big for me, that I come from a neighbourhood like this, and that I can’t afford it. What does that guy tell himself? Go ahead, might as well get into illegality, I know it pays. It doesn’t pay, guys, what it pays is bullets in the head, even when you have nothing to do with it. That’s mostly what young people need to understand. Illegality isn’t a road to follow, because it’s a path with only two endings: death or prison,” he says, quoting the French rapper Kery James.
Aujourd’hui, Arris a l’impression que le: Today, Arris feels that decision-makers think the young people of certain neighbourhoods are hopeless cases. “I don’t know if they tried and didn’t get the result they expected, and since they got nothing, they decided to give up on it. I think they tell themselves, at worst it’s Saint-Michel, who cares.” What would you like people to know? we ask him. “Don’t give up on us, don’t think we’re a lost cause, because we’re not a lost cause.
Battez-vous encore, battez-vous pour nou: Keep fighting, fight for us.” Arris doesn’t lose hope, because in his view, there are wonderful people in the neighbourhood. “For me, there are just wonderful people and there are lost people who sometimes do stupid things that are a little too big. Me, I have hope in youth, I have hope in Saint-Michel, I have hope in Montréal,” he concludes.
